name: Phenylene bis-diphenyltriazine
lead: Phenylene bis-diphenyltriazine (PBDT), also known as TriAsorB, is a synthetic UV filter that absorbs UVB and UVA radiation and, according to its developers, also high-energy visible (blue) light [1][2]. It is a triazine-class filter, listed alongside bemotrizinol and tris-biphenyl triazine in ingredient tables [3][4].

Developer-authored papers describe it as a new-generation filter with unusual optical properties and report SPF50+ formulations containing it [1][2]. The EU Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety published an opinion on its safety (listed under the code S86) [5].
Human studies are few and come largely from groups associated with its development; they examine blue-light-induced pigmentation and testing methods rather than appearance outcomes over time.
infobox: UVB, UVA and blue light (per developers) [1]

paras: The 2021 paper introducing the filter states that sunlight damage involves not only UV but also visible and infrared radiation through oxidative stress, and that a balanced protection across the spectrum is therefore sought; the authors present PBDT as a filter designed for this purpose [1]. A 2022 paper describes formulating an SPF50+ sunscreen with it for protection against UVB, UVA and blue light [2].

Separately, laboratory work using reconstructed human epidermis reported that blue light exposure reduced the repair rate of UVB-induced pyrimidine dimers, which is cited as a rationale for blue light protection [6]. Imaging studies have examined how sun filters distribute and penetrate in skin [7].

The SCCS issued an opinion on the safety of the ingredient in 2018 [5]. Review articles on visible light protection discuss it among emerging approaches, and approval status varies by jurisdiction [3][8][9].

A 2023 paper evaluated nine PBDT-containing sunscreens in vitro for blue-light photostability and photoprotection, together with a clinical evaluation of blue-light-induced skin pigmentation [10]. A separate 2023 paper described an in vivo method for evaluating sunscreen protection against high-energy visible light [11]. Both come from the filter's development context and no independent long-term trials were found.

Visible-light and blue-light protection, particularly for hyperpigmentation, is discussed in skincare communities, and this filter is mentioned as one option marketed for that purpose. No community-specific claims were found.

card.summary: Newer triazine UV filter (TriAsorB) pitched as covering blue light too; evidence is mostly developer-authored.
card.note: Blue-light claims come mainly from the filter's developers.

quick.overview:
Phenylene bis-diphenyltriazine, sold as TriAsorB, is a newer UV filter that its developers say covers UVB, UVA and blue light.

Published studies are mostly laboratory work plus a small clinical evaluation of blue-light pigmentation, largely from groups linked to its development.
quick.mechanism: It is a triazine-class absorber designed to extend sunscreen protection into the high-energy visible (blue) range as well as UV.
quick.risks: The EU SCCS published a safety opinion in 2018. No independent long-term human safety trials were found, and approval varies by jurisdiction.
